common_name: Cha-Cha Kabocha Squash (Sweet Dry-Fleshed Japanese Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; give the compact vines room to run and cure fruit for one to two weeks after harvest to fully develop sweetness.

directions: Direct sow seed in warm, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in hills with room for the moderately compact vines. Cha-Cha is a Japanese-bred kabocha-type squash that won recognition as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally sweet, dry, dense orange flesh and reliable, early, high-yielding production compared to older kabocha types. The dark green, lightly ribbed rind covers flesh that develops a rich, nutty-sweet flavor similar to roasted chestnut once cured, making it a favorite for soups, roasting, and tempura in Japanese cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage to concentrate sugars.

common_name: Baby Pam Pumpkin (Small Sweet Pie Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; give the vines room to run, and expect several small, uniform fruits per plant.

directions: Direct sow seed in warm, rich soil in full sun after the last frost, planting in hills with ample space for the vines to spread. Baby Pam is a widely grown pie pumpkin hybrid producing small, uniformly round, deep-orange fruit around 4 to 6 pounds, prized for dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh with less watery fiber than large carving pumpkins, making it excellent for pies, purees, and soups. It sets fruit reliably and uniformly across the vine, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated pie pumpkin varieties, and its handsome, deeply ribbed miniature form also works well for small-scale fall decorating. Harvest once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage.
